rejected.title: Trade-offs in environmental decisions
card: A trade-off means giving up one thing to get another. Every environmental decision has one, because no choice can deliver every benefit at no cost.
Costs and benefits can be environmental (such as habitat or clean water), economic (such as jobs or income) or social (such as health, culture or community life).
Different groups weigh these differently. Traditional Owners, local communities, developers, governments and environment groups may each give more weight to different costs and benefits.
A good decision looks at all the costs and benefits and at who gains and who loses. It does not hide what is given up.
rejected.remember: Every environmental choice gives something up, and groups may weigh the costs and benefits differently.

a.q: A council clears bushland for a new housing estate. Jobs are gained, but animal habitat is lost. What does this show?
opts: A trade-off, as jobs are gained and habitat is given up
An economic cost, as the estate creates jobs for the town
An environmental benefit, as the bush is replaced by homes
A social cost, as the new estate brings jobs and income
a.why: The council gains jobs, an economic benefit, but gives up habitat, an environmental cost. Getting one thing by giving up another is a trade-off. Calling the jobs an economic cost is tempting, but jobs are a benefit, not a cost.
a.clue: Look for what is gained and what is lost.

b.q: A town in Tasmania debates a new fish farm. It would bring jobs, but local residents and an environment group worry about water quality. Why is it hard to reach one agreed decision?
opts: Groups give different weight to jobs and water quality
Jobs are an environmental benefit that residents oppose
Water quality is an economic benefit for the farm owners
Jobs and water quality are both social costs of the farm
b.why: The jobs are an economic benefit and the risk to water quality is an environmental cost, and each group gives them different weight. Calling jobs an environmental benefit is tempting, but jobs are economic, and the residents' worry is about water, not jobs.
b.clue: Think about who gains and who loses, and how each group values it.

opts: A trade-off, as a benefit is gained and another is given up
A choice with no cost, as the homes help many people

b.q: A town in Tasmania debates a new fish farm. It would bring jobs, but local residents and an environment group worry about water quality. Why is it hard to reach one agreed decision?
opts: Groups weigh the same costs and benefits differently
Only environmental costs and benefits can be measured
The farm has benefits but no costs for anyone involved
Governments are not allowed to weigh up social costs
b.why: The jobs are an economic benefit and water quality is an environmental cost, and each group gives them different weight. The option saying the farm has no costs is wrong because every choice gives something up.
b.clue: Think about who gains and who loses, and how each group values it.
